---
title: "Git"
subtitle: "The version control that makes letting Claude edit your project safe."
---

**Git is the safety net that makes letting Claude Code edit your project
tolerable.** Without it, "Claude proposed a 200-line change across six
files" is unnerving. With it, that's just a yes/no decision: `git checkout .`
to undo, or keep the change. One keystroke either way.

This page assumes you have never really used Git. If you have a GitHub
account but only `clone` the odd repository, that counts as never.

::: {.callout-tip}
**You do not need to learn most of Git.** Rebases, cherry-picks,
submodules, hooks, the staging-area subtleties — none of it is necessary
for econ research. The handful of commands on this page are enough for
years of productive use.
:::

## The mental model in two paragraphs

Git is a **time machine** for a project folder. You decide when to take
a snapshot — that's a "commit." Every commit is permanent, locally,
forever. You can always come back to any past state. You don't need to
push to GitHub for any of this to work; "local Git" is enough to make
the snapshots and the undo path.

Each commit has a short message ("fix Table 3 standard errors"), a
date, an author, and a unique ID (a "hash" — a 7-character string like
`8dad523`). Commits form a chain. When you want to know what changed
when, undo a change from yesterday, or see what your paper looked like
three weeks ago, `git` has the answer.

## Why this matters for using Claude Code

Once an agent is editing your projects, Git earns its keep three ways:

- **Undoing.** When Claude makes an edit you don't like, `git checkout --
  file.tex` puts the file back as it was at the last commit.
- **Reading the diff.** Before accepting any non-trivial edit, you want
  to see exactly what changed. `git diff` shows you.
- **Recovering later.** When you discover a week on that a refactor broke
  a result, `git log` and `git checkout <past-hash>` take you back.

Without Git, your fail-safe is "I have a backup somewhere?" — which isn't
one. This is the [robust system](../principles.qmd) the principles page
describes, in concrete form.

## Step 1 — Confirm Git is installed

On a Mac, Git ships pre-installed. In a terminal:

```bash
git --version
```

You should see something like `git version 2.54.0`. If not, the
quickest fix is `brew install git` (if you have [Homebrew](https://brew.sh))
or downloading the installer from [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com).

On Windows: install [Git for Windows](https://gitforwindows.org/) — it
also gives you a usable bash terminal.

## Step 2 — Tell Git who you are (one-time setup)

Git records who made each commit. Configure your name and email once,
globally:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@university.edu"
```

This is metadata, not authentication. It just labels your commits.

While you're here, set the default branch name to `main` (the modern
convention) and the default editor to something you can use:

```bash
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"   # if you use VS Code
# or "nano" if you'd rather not use VS Code as your git editor
```

You only do this once per machine.

## Step 3 — Initialize a Git repo in a project

`cd` into one of your project folders (one you've already
[reorganized](reorganize-a-messy-project.qmd) — or any project you'd
like a safety net under) and:

```bash
cd ~/Desktop/wage-paper
git init
```

That's it. There's now a hidden `.git/` folder in your project that
holds the entire history. You won't ever look inside it.

Take the first snapshot, capturing the current state of everything:

```bash
git add -A
git commit -m "Initial commit"
```

Congratulations — you have a Git repository. There is now exactly one
commit. Every change you make from this point on can be reviewed,
diffed, and undone.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Run `git init` for every project, including teaching repos and
side projects.** It costs nothing and gives you the safety net
everywhere. There is no downside to having a local-only Git history.
:::

## Step 4 — The daily loop

The cycle you'll repeat constantly:

```bash
# 1. Work on your project (edit paper.tex, run analysis.do, whatever)

# 2. See what's changed since the last commit
git status

# 3. See the actual changes line-by-line
git diff

# 4. Decide what to commit. Either everything:
git add -A

# Or specific files:
git add paper.tex code/03-analysis.do

# 5. Take the snapshot
git commit -m "Update Table 3 with revised standard errors"
```

That's the whole loop. Status → diff → add → commit. Do this several
times a day, every day, on every project. Each commit is cheap and
takes seconds.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Commit messages are notes to your future self.** Treat them like the
comment line at the top of a `.do` file. "Update results" is bad;
"Fix Table 3 SE clustering at the firm level" is good. You'll thank
yourself when, six months later, you're trying to figure out which
commit broke the IV first stage.
:::

## A first session, end to end

Try this in any project:

```bash
cd ~/Desktop/some-project
git init
git add -A
git commit -m "Initial commit"

# Make a change — edit any file
echo "% added a comment" >> paper.tex

git status                    # tells you paper.tex is modified
git diff                      # shows the new line
git add paper.tex
git commit -m "Add a comment to paper.tex"

git log --oneline             # see your two commits
```

The whole thing takes two minutes. You now know enough Git to use it
every day. Everything below is for the moments when something goes
wrong — and those moments are when Git pays off most.

## Reading the past

Once you have a few commits, the questions start: "what did this
file look like last week?" "When did I change this?"

```bash
git log --oneline             # short list of every commit
git log paper.tex             # commits that touched paper.tex specifically
git show 8dad523              # the change made in commit 8dad523
git diff 8dad523              # diff against the state at commit 8dad523
git diff main~3 main          # diff between three commits ago and now
```

The `~3` notation means "three commits before"; `main~3` is "three
commits before the tip of `main`." That's the only weird syntax you'll
need for a while.

## Undoing things — the safe operations

The five operations that cover almost every "oh no" moment:

### Discard uncommitted changes to one file

You edited `paper.tex`, hated the result, want to go back to the last
committed version:

```bash
git checkout -- paper.tex
```

Or, the modern equivalent (Git 2.23+):

```bash
git restore paper.tex
```

Either way, `paper.tex` is back to its last-committed state. The file
you had on disk is gone.

::: {.callout-warning}
**This operation cannot be undone.** The version on disk is overwritten.
If the unsaved work mattered, you wanted to commit it (even on a "junk"
branch) before discarding.
:::

### Discard ALL uncommitted changes

Same idea, broader. Wipes every uncommitted edit in the working tree:

```bash
git checkout .
```

Or:

```bash
git restore .
```

This is the canonical "Claude made a mess; start over from where I was"
button.

### Unstage a file (without losing changes)

You ran `git add paper.tex` but want to take it back without losing
the edits:

```bash
git reset HEAD paper.tex
# or:
git restore --staged paper.tex
```

The file is no longer staged for the next commit, but your changes are
still on disk.

### See what a file looked like at a past commit

```bash
git show 8dad523:paper.tex > paper-from-may.tex
```

That writes the May version of `paper.tex` to a new file. You compare
to the current one without disturbing anything.

### Revert a single past commit

You committed `8dad523` last Tuesday and now want to undo just that
change, without losing anything that came after:

```bash
git revert 8dad523
```

Git creates a new commit that's the inverse of `8dad523`. Safe; doesn't
rewrite history.

## Undoing things — the destructive operations

These rewrite history. They're sometimes the right tool, but they have
sharp edges. Read carefully.

::: {.callout-warning}
**`git reset --hard <hash>`** — moves the project back to the state at
`<hash>` and **discards every commit after it.** Useful when you know
the last few commits were a mistake; dangerous when you don't.

**`git push --force`** — overwrites the remote branch with your local
state, even if it diverges. Never do this on a shared branch without
talking to coauthors first; it deletes their work from the remote.

**`git clean -fd`** — deletes every untracked file in the project.
Useful when build artifacts are everywhere; dangerous because it can
delete files Git has never seen and therefore cannot recover.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**The safety net under the destructive operations: `git reflog`.**
Every state Git has ever been in is recorded in the "reflog" for 30
days, even after `reset --hard`. If you destroy work, the first thing
to try is:

```bash
git reflog
```

That lists every state, with hashes. `git checkout <hash>` or
`git reset --hard <hash>` brings you back. It's the first thing to reach
for when you think you've lost work.
:::

## Branches — for trying things without breaking what works

Branches are alternate timelines. Useful for "let me try this big
refactor without messing up the current paper draft."

```bash
git checkout -b experiment        # create and switch to a new branch
# … work, commit, work, commit …
git checkout main                 # back to the main timeline
git merge experiment              # bring the experiment's commits into main
```

If you decide the experiment was a bad idea:

```bash
git checkout main
git branch -D experiment          # throw it away
```

For solo research projects, you'll often skip branches entirely and
just commit to `main`. That's fine. Use branches when:

- You want to try a structural change you might roll back.
- You're collaborating and want to share work-in-progress without
  disturbing the main line.
- You're preparing a replication package while still working on
  follow-ups.

::: {.callout-note}
**Merging is straightforward when nobody else has changed the same
lines you did.** When two people edit the same line, you get a "merge
conflict" — Git asks you to choose between (or combine) the two
versions. Don't panic; this is a normal part of collaboration. Claude
Code is good at walking you through resolving conflicts. See
"[When you're stuck](#when-youre-stuck)" below.
:::

## Worktrees — when one working directory isn't enough

A **worktree** is a second (or third) working directory that shares the
same `.git` repository. Each worktree sits on its own branch. You can
edit, commit, run scripts in any worktree independently — but the
underlying history is shared, so commits in one show up in the other
the moment you pull or fetch.

This is *not* day-one Git. It is, however, the feature you'll wish you
had once you have a long-running project, coauthors, and Claude Code
all in the same workflow.

### The basic mechanics

From inside your existing project:

```bash
git worktree add ../paper-revision revision-2026
```

That creates a new directory at `../paper-revision`, checked out on
branch `revision-2026` (created if it doesn't exist). Your **original
working directory is unchanged** — you can keep working in it. Open the
new one in another VS Code window and you have two parallel checkouts
of the same project.

When you're done with the second worktree:

```bash
git worktree remove ../paper-revision
git branch -D revision-2026     # if you don't want to keep the branch
```

### When you'd actually want this

1. **Working on two branches without context-switching.** You're
   mid-revision on `revision-2026` when a referee email arrives asking
   a quick question about a result on `main`. Without worktrees you'd
   `git stash` (which loses your editor state and any half-typed
   prompts to Claude), `git checkout main`, answer, switch back, `git
   stash pop`. With worktrees: open the `main` worktree in another
   window, answer there, never disturb the revision work.

2. **Long-running jobs you can't interrupt.** A Stata batch job is
   running in your project's main checkout. Switching branches
   mid-job is risky — the script might pick up the wrong files
   partway through. A worktree on a different branch lets you do
   exploratory work in parallel without touching the running job.

3. **Side-by-side comparison.** Open the old version in one window,
   the new version in another. Especially useful for paper revisions:
   when you're writing a response-to-referees, you can keep the
   submitted text and the revised text both on screen at once. Same
   trick for code: the published replication's `analysis.do` in one
   window, your in-progress revision in another.

4. **Reorganizing a project without copying.** The
   [reorganize-a-messy-project walkthrough](reorganize-a-messy-project.qmd)
   recommends `cp -R` for git novices, but a worktree is a strict
   improvement when you're git-fluent and the original is already in
   git. The reorganization shows up as a series of commits on a
   branch; `git diff main..reorganize-2026` reviews the whole change
   at the end.

5. **Letting Claude work in isolation.** Claude Code's Agent tool can
   spawn a sub-agent in its own worktree (the `isolation: "worktree"`
   option), so a disruptive task — a big refactor, a structural
   rewrite, an experimental rewrite of your tables — runs in a
   parallel checkout while you keep working in your main one. The
   agent reports back what it changed; you decide whether to merge.
   Without worktrees, the same task would either lock you out of your
   project for the duration or leave you wondering whether the agent's
   half-finished state is corrupting what you're looking at.

6. **Multi-version verification.** You want to confirm a result
   reproduces in both Stata 17 and Stata 18, or in both R 4.3 and R
   4.4. A worktree per version with the relevant environment files
   committed lets you keep both setups warm at the same time.

### Listing and pruning

```bash
git worktree list                  # show every worktree this repo has
git worktree prune                 # clean up stale references
```

`git worktree list` is the answer to "wait, did I create that other
worktree six months ago and forget about it?"

### Things to be careful about

- **Each worktree must be on a different branch.** You can't have two
  worktrees on `main` at the same time.
- **Don't `rm -rf` a worktree folder.** Use `git worktree remove`
  instead — otherwise Git keeps stale references and you'll need to
  clean up with `git worktree prune` later.
- **Don't put worktrees inside Dropbox / iCloud / OneDrive.** Same
  sync-conflict reasons as putting your main project there.
- **Each worktree has its own untracked files.** Things in
  `.gitignore` (build artifacts, derived data) are not shared between
  worktrees — each one builds its own.
- **Submodules and global git config are shared.** Hooks, configured
  identity, etc., are repo-wide.

## Going beyond your machine — GitHub

Everything above works with **zero internet connection**. Git is
purely local. To back up your work, share with coauthors, or publish
a replication package, you push to a "remote" — usually GitHub
([github.com](https://github.com)) but GitLab, Bitbucket, and
self-hosted alternatives work the same way.

### One-time setup per project

Create an empty repository on GitHub. It will give you a URL like
`https://github.com/yourname/wage-paper.git`. In your local project:

```bash
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/wage-paper.git
git push -u origin main
```

The `-u origin main` part is shorthand for "remember that my local
`main` corresponds to `main` on `origin`" — you only need it the first
time.

### The everyday loop, with a remote

When you're working from one machine on a solo project, you don't need
to push every time. When you do push:

```bash
git push                    # send your commits to GitHub
git pull                    # fetch coauthors' commits and merge in
```

That's the whole remote workflow. The vast majority of "Git frustration"
in econ comes from forgetting to `git pull` before starting work — when
you do, your commits and your coauthor's commits diverge, and you have
to do a merge.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Do not push your projects to a public GitHub repo without thinking
about what's in them.** Anything in `data/raw/` may include
restricted-access or IRB-protected data. Anything in your code may
include hardcoded paths revealing folder structures you'd rather not
share. Default to **private** repos and only flip to public deliberately
when you're ready to publish a replication package. See
[Confidential data](../pitfalls/confidential-data.qmd).
:::

## Coauthor workflow

Two coauthors editing the same project, each with their own laptop and
a shared GitHub repo:

1. **Always `git pull` before you start working.** This brings their
   commits into your local copy.
2. **Commit and push when you stop for the day.** Tiny commits with
   real messages are infinitely better than one big "Update" commit at
   the end of the week.
3. **If a `git pull` produces a merge conflict**, Git will tell you
   exactly which files conflict. Open them; you'll see markers like:

    ```
    <<<<<<< HEAD
    your version
    =======
    your coauthor's version
    >>>>>>> main
    ```

    Pick which one survives (or combine them), delete the markers,
    `git add`, `git commit`. Done.
4. **Communicate before doing anything destructive on a shared
   branch.** No `git push --force`, no `git reset --hard` of pushed
   commits, without a Slack/email/text first.

For most coauthorships, that's it. You don't need branches per
collaborator unless the project gets complex.

## What NOT to commit

A `.gitignore` file at the project root tells Git to skip these. The
[reorganize page's Step 12](reorganize-a-messy-project.qmd#step-12-add-gitignore)
has a full template; the highlights:

- **Large data files.** GitHub's free tier limits files to 100 MB and
  repos to a soft 1 GB. For large datasets, use [Git LFS](https://git-lfs.github.com/)
  or store the data outside the repo and document where it lives in
  the README.
- **Restricted-access or confidential data.** Never commit it, full
  stop. See [Confidential data](../pitfalls/confidential-data.qmd).
- **Secrets / credentials.** API keys, database passwords, anything
  ending in `.pem` or `.key`. If you ever commit one by accident,
  treat it as compromised and rotate it.
- **Derived outputs.** `data/derived/`, `output/tables/*.tex`,
  `paper/paper.pdf`. These are reproducible from the source — no
  reason to track them.
- **Build artifacts.** `.aux`, `.log`, `.synctex.gz`, `*.smcl`,
  `__pycache__/`, `.Rhistory`, etc.

## The friendly path: VS Code's Source Control pane

If you'd rather use Git through a graphical interface, the best one is
**already inside VS Code**. Open the Source Control pane
(`Ctrl+Shift+G` or click the branching-tree icon in the left sidebar).
You'll see:

- A list of every changed file, grouped by "Staged" and "Changes."
- Click any file to see the diff in the editor — same diff `git diff`
  prints, but pretty.
- The `+` next to a file stages it. The `-` un-stages it.
- The text box at the top is the commit message; the checkmark icon
  commits.
- The `…` menu has push, pull, branch operations, etc.

If you'd rather not touch the CLI for Git, this is the recommended path.
The same operations happen under the hood; you just click instead of
typing. See the [VS Code page](vscode.qmd) for the broader VS Code setup.

::: {.callout-note}
**Other graphical Git clients** worth knowing about: GitHub Desktop
(simplest; free; opinionated), GitKraken (powerful; free for academic
use), Sourcetree (free; aging). All are fine. If you're already in
VS Code, you don't need any of them.
:::

## What Claude Code does with Git on your behalf

Claude Code knows Git. When working in a project with `git init`-d
already, it will:

- Run `git status` and `git diff` on its own to see what's changed.
- Stage and commit files when you ask.
- Create branches if you ask.
- Read history with `git log` to understand the project's evolution.

It will **not**:

- Run `git push` without you asking explicitly.
- Run any destructive operation (`reset --hard`, `clean -fd`,
  `push --force`) without prompting first.
- Commit changes silently. By default, you see what it staged before
  the commit happens.

A useful default is to **let Claude commit on your behalf for routine
work** ("commit the bibliography fix you just made"), but
**type `git push` yourself** the first time it goes to a shared remote.
Pushes are visible to other people; that one's worth a conscious
keypress.

## When you're stuck

The "I think I broke Git" recovery path:

1. **Stop. Don't run more commands.** The single most common way to
   make a Git problem worse is to keep running `git` commands hoping
   one of them fixes it.
2. **Run `git status`** and read what it says. Git's error messages,
   for all their reputation, are usually accurate and tell you the
   next command to run.
3. **`git reflog` is your "undo undo."** Every state Git has been in is
   recorded for 30 days. If you destroyed something, it's almost
   certainly in there. Find the hash you want; `git checkout <hash>`
   to inspect, `git reset --hard <hash>` to fully restore.
4. **Ask Claude.** Open Claude Code in the project, paste the output
   of `git status` and `git reflog`, and say what you were trying to
   do when things went wrong. Claude is genuinely good at Git
   diagnosis — it's seen every variation of "I made a mess" before.

## What you can safely skip

Rebase, cherry-pick, stash, submodules, and hooks are all real tools, but
none are on your critical path for econ research — pick them up the day
you actually need one. The [Pro Git book](https://git-scm.com/book) covers
them when you're ready. The one to keep at arm's length is
`git push --force` on a shared branch: it can delete coauthors' commits,
so never run it without a talked-through agreement (and prefer
`git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses to overwrite work you didn't
know about).
